name: Kurjey Lhakhang
significance: A three-temple monastery complex in Bhutan's Bumthang valley, the oldest of whose shrines was raised by king Sindhu Raja beside a meditation cave. It also serves as the resting place of the remains of Bhutan's first three kings.
story: Oral tradition holds that Padmasambhava subdued the local deity Shelging Karpo here and left the imprint of his body in the cave, from which the site takes its name.

name: Gangteng Monastery
significance: Founded in 1613 by Gyalse Pema Thinley, grandson of the treasure-revealer Pema Lingpa, this fortress-like monastery above the Phobjikha valley is the principal seat of the Pema Lingpa tradition and one of Bhutan's two main Nyingma centres. It was extensively restored between 2002 and 2008 with the support of the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck.
story: Local accounts tell that a guardian deity caused a landslide that exposed the stone needed to build the monastery, and that the valley's black-necked cranes circle it three times on arrival and again before returning to Tibet.

name: Buddha Dordenma
significance: A 54-metre bronze Shakyamuni Buddha seated on a hill above Thimphu, cast by the Aerosun Corporation of Nanjing and completed on 25 September 2015 to mark the sixtieth anniversary of King Jigme Singye Wangchuck. Its base houses some 100,000 smaller bronze Buddha images.
story: The statue is held to fulfil a prophecy attributed to the 20th-century yogi Sonam Zangpo, and an older terma of Guru Rinpoche, that a great image would be raised in Bhutan to bestow blessings, peace and happiness.

name: Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi
deity: Sacred Bodhi tree of the Buddha
significance: A sacred fig grown from a cutting of the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, planted in the royal park at Anuradhapura in 288 BCE by King Devanampiya Tissa and protected by later rulers including Vasabha, Sena II and Kirti Sri Rajasinha. Raised on a terrace some 6.5 metres above ground and ringed by walls and companion trees, it draws millions of pilgrims a year.
story: Sri Lankan tradition holds that the southern branch of the original Bodhi tree was carried to the island by the Buddhist nun Sanghamitta, daughter of the emperor Ashoka.

name: Dambulla Cave Temple
significance: Five rock-cut caves on a granite outcrop that King Valagamba converted into a monastery in the first century BCE, gilded and filled with some seventy Buddha images by Nissanka Malla in 1190, and painted under the Kandyan king Kirti Sri Rajasinha in the 18th century. Inscribed by UNESCO in 1991, it is the best-preserved ancient monastic complex in Sri Lanka and remains in use.
story: Local tradition credits Vishnu with creating the caves by divine power, and holds that the water dripping in the second cave has healing power.

name: Mihintale
deity: Gautama Buddha; associated with Arahant Mahinda
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE onwards; additions to 10th c.
significance: A hill of stupas, drip-ledged caves and monastic ruins near Anuradhapura where, by chronicle tradition, the monk Mahinda met King Devanampiyatissa on the Poson full-moon day and preached the Buddha's doctrine, marking the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka. Its inscriptions and structures span the 3rd century BCE to the 10th century CE, with works recorded under rulers from Suratissa to Mihindu.
story: The Mahavamsa relates that Mahinda travelled through the air and alighted on the rock of Aradhana Gala, where he first met the king.

name: Kelaniya Raja Maha Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple on the Kelani river near Colombo, traditionally traced to the Naga king Maniakkika and closely bound up with the fortunes of successive Sri Lankan states. It was patronised by the Kandyan king Kirti Sri Rajasingha and refurbished in the early 20th century with support from Helena Wijewardene.
story: Buddhist tradition holds that the Buddha visited Kelaniya in the eighth year after his enlightenment to settle a dispute, and that the Naga kings afterwards enshrined the gem-studded throne he had used.

name: Gal Vihara
significance: A face of granite gneiss at Polonnaruwa carved with four large Buddha images, seated, standing and reclining, commissioned by King Parakramabahu I in the 12th century. He convened a monastic council here to reconcile the island's three fraternities and had the resulting code of conduct cut into the rock; the figures are regarded as high points of Sinhalese sculpture.

name: Jetavanaramaya
builtDisplay: begun 3rd c. under Mahasena, completed by Kithsirimevan
significance: A colossal brick stupa at Anuradhapura begun by King Mahasena in the late 3rd century and finished by his son Kithsirimevan, raised amid the rivalry between the Mahavihara and Mahayana factions. At about 122 metres it was once the tallest stupa in the world and among the tallest structures of antiquity; Parakramabahu I renovated it in the 12th century.
story: A piece of a sash worn by the Buddha is believed to be the relic enshrined within it, and the surrounding forest is said to be named Jetavana after the grove where Mahinda preached.

name: Abhayagiri Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha; once housed the Tooth Relic
significance: One of the great monastic cities of ancient Anuradhapura, whose dagaba was raised by King Valagamba during his second reign in the late 1st century BCE and which grew into a centre where Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana learning coexisted. Its monks maintained scholarly links with China, Java and Kashmir, and from the 4th century the Buddha's Tooth Relic was shown here.
story: Tradition relates that Valagamba, taunted by a Jain ascetic named Giri as he fled a battle, vowed to build a monastery on the spot and fulfilled the oath fourteen years later on regaining his throne.

name: Munneswaram Temple
builtDisplay: attested by c. 1000 CE; present form 1753
significance: A Shiva temple complex near Chilaw attested at least since about 1000 CE and patronised in turn by the kings of Kotte, Sitawaka and Kandy, reaching its present form under Kirti Sri Rajasinghe in 1753. One of the island's Pancha Ishwaram shrines, it comprises five structures including a Buddhist temple, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Aiyanar and Kali.
story: Tamil tradition links the temple to Rama of the Ramayana, while Sinhala Buddhist myth tells of the goddess Kali coming ashore at Chilaw and settling at Munneswaram, where the deity Pattini restrained her from harming people.

name: Naguleswaram Temple
significance: The northernmost of Sri Lanka's Pancha Ishwaram Shiva temples, standing beside the Keerimalai springs north of Jaffna and counted among the oldest shrines of the region. Destroyed by the Portuguese in 1621 and restored by Arumuka Navalar in 1894, it was bombed during the civil war and reconstructed by February 2012.
story: The sage Nagula Muni, whose body had shrivelled from austerities, is said to have been cured by bathing in the springs and to have founded the shrine to the lingam in gratitude.

name: Seetha Amman Temple
significance: A Vaishnavite temple to Sita at Seetha Eliya near Nuwara Eliya, grown from a simple site where unshaped stones stood for the deities into a full temple built by South Indian Tamil plantation workers, who still maintain it. It is a principal stop on Sri Lanka's Ramayana pilgrimage circuit and has been promoted by Ramayana advocacy groups in India.
story: The Ramayana places Sita's captivity under Ravana at this spot and holds that Hanuman found her here and gave her Rama's ring as a token of hope.

name: Shri Varun Dev Mandir
significance: A temple on Manora Island off Karachi, said to be the only shrine dedicated to Varuna in Pakistan and of particular importance to Sindhi Hindus. Its present structure was renovated around 1917-18 and the building was restored again in 2018 by the Sindh Exploration and Adventure Society.
story: Tradition holds that the temple was commissioned around the 16th century after the wealthy sailor Bhojomal Nenshi Bhatia bought Manora Island from the Khan of Kalat.

name: Panchmukhi Hanuman Temple
significance: A Hindu temple in Soldier Bazaar, Karachi, holding a 2.5-metre five-faced Hanuman image and protected as a national heritage site under the Sindh Cultural Heritage (Preservation) Act of 1994. Renovation begun in 2012 and further work in 2019 uncovered more centuries-old statuary at the site.
story: Devotees hold that Rama visited this spot during his exile and that the Hanuman image here was divinely revealed rather than made by human hands.

name: Goraknath Temple
significance: A Hindu temple at the centre of the Gor Khatri compound in Peshawar, dedicated to Guru Gorakhnath, founder of the Kanphata Jogi order, and dated to 1851. Closed for decades, it was reopened in 2011 on the order of the Peshawar High Court and declared a heritage site; it is one of very few Hindu temples still standing in the city.

name: Mankiala Stupa
significance: A large Buddhist stupa on the Potohar plateau south-east of Rawalpindi, associated by inscription with the Kushan emperor Kanishka, who is recorded as having visited it often. It was described by Mountstuart Elphinstone in his memoir of 1815 and opened in 1830 by Jean-Baptiste Ventura, whose relic finds were removed to the British Museum under British rule.
story: Jataka tradition holds that the stupa marks the spot where Prince Sattva, an earlier birth of the Buddha, gave parts of his own body to feed seven starving tiger cubs.

name: Jandial Temple
significance: A temple opposite the ruined city of Sirkap at Taxila, excavated in 1912-13 by John Marshall for the Archaeological Survey of India. Laid out like a Greek temple with naos, pronaos and opisthodomos and fronted by finely cut Ionic columns, it is the most Hellenic structure yet found in Pakistan, though its dedication and patron remain disputed.

name: Sadh Belo
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Annapurna, Hanuman and Ganesha
significance: A temple complex on an island in the Indus at Sukkur, settled in 1823 by the Udasi ascetic Baba Bankhandi Maharaj and built up from 1899 under the eighth gaddi nashin Sant Harnam Das. Its Teerath Asthan is described as the largest Hindu temple in Pakistan, and the annual Bankhandi Maharaj mela draws thousands of pilgrims for three days of free lodging and food.
story: Bankhandi is said to have been visited in a dream by the goddess Annapurna, who gave him a kamandal with the promise that while it stayed on the island the community kitchen would never lack grain.

name: Mes Aynak
significance: An extensive ancient Buddhist settlement in Logar province with monasteries, dwellings and more than 400 Buddha statues spread over some 40 hectares, at its height between the 5th and 7th centuries CE. Coins of the Alchon rulers Khingila and Mehama date part of the occupation to around 450-500 CE; the site declined from the 8th century and has since been excavated under the threat of copper mining.

name: Takht-e Rostam
significance: A Buddhist stupa and monastery near Samangan hewn entirely out of the bedrock in the 3rd-4th centuries CE under the Kushano-Sasanians. After the Muslim conquests the abandoned complex was absorbed into Persian legend, which supplied its present name.
story: Persian tradition holds that the hero Rostam of Ferdowsi's Shahnameh travelled to the kingdom of Samangan and stayed with its king at this place.

name: Adinath Temple, Maheshkhali
significance: A Shiva temple on the summit of Mainak hill on Maheshkhali island off Cox's Bazar. It is best known for the thirteen-day fair held at the foot of the hill in the month of Phalgun, which draws thousands of pilgrims from across Bangladesh.

name: Puthia Temple Complex
deity: Krishna, Shiva and Jagannath across several temples
significance: The largest cluster of historic Hindu temples in Bangladesh, raised at Puthia in Rajshahi by the zamindars and rajas of the Puthia Raj family, whose estate was established in the 16th century. It includes the Pancha Ratna Govinda temple, the Bhubaneshwar Shiva temple built by Rani Bhubonmoyee Devi in 1823, and several smaller shrines faced with terracotta ornament.

name: Ramna Kali Mandir
significance: A Kali temple in the Ramna area of Dhaka, first raised in the Mughal period and much enlarged in the early 20th century under Rani Bilashmoni Debi, when it stood among the city's tallest landmarks. The complex was destroyed by the Pakistan Army on 27 March 1971 during the Liberation War; the rebuilt temple was inaugurated on 17 December 2021.
story: Nepalese folklore holds that the devotees who founded the temple had come to Bengal from the Himalayas.

name: Shalban Vihara
significance: A square Buddhist monastery of 115 monastic cells around a central shrine on the Mainamati-Lalmai ridge near Comilla, attributed to Bhava Deva, the fourth ruler of the early Deva dynasty. It remained in use into the 12th century and excavation has yielded artefacts spanning the 7th to 12th centuries.

name: Mahasthangarh
deity: Ancient city and Buddhist monastic site (Vasu Vihara)
significance: A fortified ancient city near Bogra identified with Pundranagara, capital of the Pundra kingdom, occupied from not later than the 3rd century BCE until its fortified area fell out of use in the 8th century CE. Excavations in and around the citadel, including the Buddhist monastery of Vasu Vihara, have exposed remains of the Mauryan, Gupta and later periods.
story: Local tradition tells of the saint Shah Sultan Balkhi Mahisawar, who arrived riding a fish and defeated King Parasuram after having the Jiat Kunda pool, whose water revived the king's fallen soldiers, contaminated so that it lost its power.

name: Sulamani Temple
significance: A brick-and-stone temple at Bagan built in 1183 by King Narapatisithu, close in design to the Thatbyinnyu, influenced by the Dhammayangyi and in turn a model for the later Htilominlo. Damaged by the earthquake of 1975 and rebuilt in 1994, it retains interior frescoes and is one of Bagan's most visited monuments.

name: Dhammayangyi Temple
significance: The largest and widest temple at Bagan, begun by King Narathu in 1167 and left unfinished when he was assassinated three years later. Its inner corridors were bricked up at some later point for reasons never established, so only the outer passages can be entered.
story: The chronicles say Narathu came to the throne by killing his father and elder brother, and that he raised this vast temple to atone for those crimes.

name: Thatbyinnyu Temple
significance: The tallest temple at Bagan, a five-storeyed brick and stucco structure about 61 metres high crowned by a sikhara tower, completed in 1150-51 in the reign of King Sithu I. It is read by scholars as a high point of Pagan-period architecture, and has been under restoration since the earthquake of 2016.

name: Htilominlo Temple
significance: A three-storeyed red-brick temple 46 metres high at Bagan, completed in 1211 under King Htilominlo, also known as Nandaungmya. Four Buddha images face the cardinal directions on its ground floor, and it is noted for its elaborate plaster mouldings.

name: Sule Pagoda
builtDisplay: enlarged 15th c. under Shin Sawbu; traditionally far older
significance: An octagonal gilded stupa about 44 metres high at the centre of downtown Yangon, whose main structure was enlarged by Queen Shin Sawbu between 1453 and 1472. When Lt. Alexander Fraser laid out the colonial street grid in the mid-19th century he made the pagoda its hub, and it has since served as a rallying point in the 1988 and 2007 uprisings.
story: Legend says the nat Sularata, whose eyelids had to be propped open, showed King Okkalapa where three earlier Buddhas had buried relics, and the pagoda was raised there over a hair of the Buddha given to the merchants Trapusa and Bahalika.

name: Botataung Pagoda
significance: A riverside pagoda in Yangon, destroyed by Allied bombing on 8 November 1943 and rebuilt from 4 January 1948, the day of Myanmar's independence. Clearing the ruins uncovered a relic chamber whose contents, including what is venerated as a hair of the Buddha, are now displayed inside the hollow, walk-through stupa.
story: Its name, meaning a thousand military officers, is said to come from the thousand officers who formed a guard of honour when relics of the Buddha were brought here from India more than two thousand years ago.

name: Kuthodaw Pagoda
significance: A stupa and inscription complex at the foot of Mandalay Hill begun by King Mindon Min in 1860, its 57-metre main stupa modelled on the Shwezigon at Nyaung-U. Its 729 marble slabs, each housed in a small shrine, carry the Tipitaka in stone and are often called the world's largest book; they were opened to the public in 1868 and served the Fifth Buddhist Synod.

name: Shwenandaw Monastery
significance: A teak monastery in Mandalay created in 1878, when King Thibaw Min had his father King Mindon's former royal apartment taken down and re-erected outside the palace as a memorial. It is the only major original structure of the Mandalay royal palace still standing.
story: Thibaw is said to have moved the building because he believed it haunted by his father's spirit; he used it for meditation, and the couch on which he sat is still shown there.

name: Shite-thaung Temple
significance: A fortress-like temple on the western face of Pokhaung hill at Mrauk U, built in 1535-36 by King Min Bin to commemorate his conquest of Bengal. Known as the Temple of 80,000 Buddha Images and also as the Temple of Victory, it has a central bell-shaped stupa with four corner stupas and three concentric maze-like corridors lined with Buddha figures and relief carving.

name: Kaunghmudaw Pagoda
significance: A white stupa 46 metres high near Sagaing, built between April 1636 and May 1648 under King Thalun of the Restored Toungoo kingdom. Its formal name Yaza Mani Sula refers to the relics enshrined in its chamber, and its rounded, egg-shaped dome, modelled on the Ruwanwelisaya in Sri Lanka, sets it apart from the usual Burmese bell profile.
story: Local belief holds that the relic chamber contains the Buddha's lower left tooth, eleven hair relics and an alms bowl, and that the dome was raised around a 7.3-metre marble Buddha image.

name: Wat Phra Si Sanphet
significance: The royal chapel of the Ayutthaya palace, made a sacred precinct by King Borommatrailokkanat in 1448 on the site of the palace founded by Ramathibodi I in 1350, and marked by three bell-shaped chedis raised between 1492 and 1529. Reserved for the royal family and once housing an enormous gold-covered Buddha, it was destroyed in the Burmese sack of 1767.

name: Wat Mahathat, Ayutthaya
significance: A royal relic monastery in the centre of Ayutthaya, recorded in the royal chronicles as founded in 1374 by Borommarachathirat I together with the elder Thammakanlayan and expanded ten years later by his nephew Ramesuan. Now a ruin, it is among the most important temple sites of the UNESCO-listed historic city.

name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
significance: A riverside temple west of Ayutthaya island completed in 1630 as the first foundation of King Prasat Thong's reign, in memory of his mother's residence there. Built to a Khmer plan with a 35-metre central prang ringed by four lesser prangs and eight chedi-shaped chapels carrying Jataka reliefs, it lay abandoned after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767 until restoration began in 1987.

name: Wat Traimit
deity: Gautama Buddha (Phra Phuttha Maha Suwanna Patimakon, the Golden Buddha)
significance: A temple in Bangkok's Chinatown, probably founded in the reign of Rama III, largely rebuilt in the 1930s-40s and renamed Wat Traimit Witthayaram in 1940. It enshrines the Phra Phuttha Maha Suwanna Patimakon, a solid-gold Buddha brought here in 1935 whose gold core came to light only when the plaster covering it broke during a move in 1955; the image now sits in a four-storey marble-clad mondop.
story: Oral history holds that the temple was founded by three Chinese friends, which is said to explain its name.

name: Wat Saket
builtDisplay: 19th c.; Golden Mount completed under Rama V
significance: A Bangkok temple of Ayutthaya-period origin, known as Wat Sakae until King Rama I renovated and renamed it, and crowned by the Golden Mount, an artificial hill and chedi begun under Rama III and completed under Rama V. Through the 19th century it was the city's principal cremation ground, overwhelmed by the dead during the cholera epidemics between 1820 and 1881.
story: The vultures of Wat Saket, the flocks that fed on corpses left exposed during those epidemics, passed into Bangkok speech as a byword for death and gave rise to ghost stories about the place.
